items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I thought maybe there was a chance along the way there was going to be some pop music in my future, of performing my own songs and being Billy Joel or James Taylor.

ctx.x: Did you get to a point on a particular day or time when you said you know I’m going to make my living doing this?

You know I never did. The only thing that I wanted to do I thought was to — I thought somewhere along the line a wrote a lot of pop songs and I thought maybe there was a chance along the way there was going to be some pop music in my future, of performing my own songs and being Billy Joel or James Taylor. And it’s interesting you should ask that question because I never ever realized that I was making a living doing what I was — and I was playing with my dad, and I’d be getting these $600 checks and $1000 checks…
What was your repertoire at the time? CCR and that kind of stuff?

items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And so James called me, so it only took him twenty-some-odd years before — no, about seventeen years later he texted me and said, “I want to do a record of standards and you da man” it said.

ctx.x: Well we did — the first part was Russ Titelman called me to play, do a date for him in August of 2001. And it was down at Clinton. And he had a song called “Mean Old Man.” And I was in the booth with my guitar and James came into the thing and he was showing me the chords. They had sort of a nutty chord sheet and James came in and he went — and he always whistles like, playing all the chords. And I’m going this is James Taylor sitting in front of me. And I could see Russ Titelman on the other side, outside the…

Goldings played piano and Steve Gadd was the drummer. And I remember when I played the track for Bucky, I said, “Hey listen to this.” So he heard the thing and then the second he heard [sings] the first chunk he said, “Who’s the rhythm player?” I said, “Thank you very much.” I said, I passed the test. So James said something to me like, “Well you’ve got to show me how you do that rhythm thing, that’s really great.” I mean he really liked the rhythm guitar. And I said to him, “Well you can show me that finger…

sing like Little Richard or Elvis when I sing rock & roll. But here I am singing standards. I don’t know who to sing like. And it was really cool. So with James Taylor he knew it was going to be James Taylorized. He just wanted to make sure it was within — you know he really had a — he was really smart. They both were smart, I mean they are both geniuses in their own little way.
